title: The Story of Chess
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Chess is one of the oldest games still played today. Its ancestor, a game called chaturanga, appeared in India around the sixth century. The name means 'four divisions', a reference to the four parts of an Indian army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots, which later became the pawn, the knight, the bishop and the rook. The game was played on an eight-by-eight board, and it was valued as a way of teaching the art of war to young princes. Pieces were carved from wood, ivory and stone, and sets made for kings were often works of art.

From India the game spread to Persia, where it was called shatranj, and the Persians introduced the call 'shah', meaning king, which survives in our word 'check'. After the Arab conquest of Persia in the seventh century, Muslim players carried the game across North Africa to Spain, and by about the year 1000 it was being played in most of Europe. Travelling merchants, soldiers and pilgrims all helped to spread it, and so, many historians believe, did the trade routes of Central Asia.

The rules changed as the game moved west. In the early game the queen, then called the counsellor, could move only one square at a time, and the bishop could jump only two squares diagonally. Around 1475, in Spain or Italy, the two pieces gained their modern powers, and the game became much faster and more exciting. Other rules, such as castling and the first move of two squares for a pawn, were added over the following century, until the game looked very much as it does today. For a time, in some countries, it was known as 'the mad queen's chess'.

Chess grew into a serious competition in the nineteenth century. The first international tournament was held in London in 1851, and in 1886 Wilhelm Steinitz became the first official world champion. In 1924, an international federation, FIDE, was founded in Paris to organise tournaments and to agree the rules. Today it has about two hundred member countries, and the best players travel the world to compete for prizes, titles and fame.

The mathematics of the game is astonishing. After only a few moves each, there are millions of possible positions, and the number of possible games is estimated to be greater than the number of atoms in the observable universe. No player, however gifted, can calculate everything, so players rely on pattern recognition, which they develop through years of study. Research suggests that a strong player may recognise around fifty thousand patterns at a glance. This is why a master can often take in a position in seconds, while a beginner sees only a crowd of pieces and has to count each one.

Computers have changed chess completely. In 1997, an IBM computer called Deep Blue defeated the world champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match in New York, the first time that a machine had beaten a reigning champion in a match under tournament conditions. Today, a free program on a mobile phone plays better than any human. Instead of ending the game, however, the machines have become teachers: young players use them to analyse their games and to find ideas that no coach had imagined.

Interest in chess has grown rapidly in recent years. During the lockdowns of 2020, millions of people learned the game online, helped by the popularity of a television series, The Queen's Gambit. Schools in many countries, including Armenia, now teach chess as a lesson, because teachers believe that it improves concentration and logical thinking. The evidence for this is mixed, but nobody doubts that the game is a pleasure to play, and that it can be learned at any age.
